Variants.Content: Ranking among Byzantium's wealthiest dynastic magnates, the House of Kantakouzenos held large estates in Smyrna, Thrace, and the Anatolian interior. The family fielded private retinues and lent gold to the Nicaean crown, and its commanders often held the office of Megas Domestikos, the commander of the field army. Michael VIII relied on Kantakouzenos generals in his campaigns, and their support helped him reclaim Constantinople in 1261. Their estates were tied to the monastic houses of the Aegean, which made the family a patron of scribes and scholars. Their wealth made them a counterweight to the emperor's own treasury.

Intermarrying with the Palaiologoi, Kantakouzenos generals steered imperial military policy and balanced aristocratic privileges against the emperor's need for centralized revenue. Each marriage contract brought lands and fortresses into the family's hands, and the emperor's secretaries recorded every such grant in the registers.
Their fortified estates patronized monastic scriptoriums, copying classical philosophy and patristic commentaries amid turbulent Anatolian frontier warfare.
